failure_modes.description: The assumption that local reward functions align with global traffic objectives is fundamentally flawed without a centralized coordination mechanism to ensure alignment.
failure_modes.evidence: Traffic networks are inherently non-linear systems where local optimizations often create global bottlenecks (Braess paradox). Without explicit alignment between local and global objectives, the system will inevitably create worse overall performance.

failure_modes.description: This contradicts decades of traffic engineering research showing that network-wide coordination is necessary for optimal traffic flow.
failure_modes.evidence: Modern traffic control systems (SCATS, SCOOT) all rely on some form of centralized coordination or network-wide optimization. Pure decentralized approaches have consistently failed in real-world implementations.

failure_modes.description: The hypothesis fails to account for boundary conditions where intersections have asymmetric traffic patterns or different road capacities.
failure_modes.evidence: In heterogeneous networks where intersections have vastly different traffic characteristics, the learning mechanism would converge at different rates, potentially creating bottlenecks at intersections with higher computational complexity.

failure_modes.description: This approach is not novel as similar multi-agent reinforcement learning approaches have been attempted and failed in traffic control.
failure_modes.evidence: Previous implementations of multi-agent RL for traffic control (e.g., Van der Pol et al. 2018) consistently showed that without significant constraints or network awareness, systems either failed to converge or performed worse than traditional methods.

failure_modes.description: The expected failure modes (oscillations, local optima) are not just possible but inevitable in this design.
failure_modes.evidence: The described mechanism guarantees oscillations because intersections will continuously respond to local conditions without awareness of network-wide effects, creating a classic 'tragedy of the commons' scenario where each intersection optimizes for itself at the expense of the network.

failure_modes.description: The computational requirements for real-time policy evaluation at each intersection are incompatible with the processing capabilities of existing traffic signal controllers.
failure_modes.evidence: Modern traffic signal controllers typically have limited computational resources (often 8-16 bit processors) incapable of running complex reinforcement learning algorithms in real-time while handling other critical functions like pedestrian detection and emergency vehicle preemption.
